topicName: Fast and slow twitch muscle fibres

cards.front: What is the main difference between slow twitch and fast twitch muscle fibres?
cards.back: **Slow twitch** fibres contract slowly and resist fatigue, whereas **fast twitch** fibres contract quickly and powerfully but tire sooner.

cards.front: Why can slow twitch fibres keep working for hours without tiring?
cards.back: They make most of their ATP by **aerobic respiration**, using many mitochondria, myoglobin and capillaries, so lactate builds up slowly.
cards.hint: Think about which respiration type needs a steady oxygen supply.

cards.front: Why do fast twitch fibres suit short, explosive movements such as sprinting?
cards.back: They release ATP very quickly by **anaerobic respiration** using glycogen and phosphocreatine, which is faster than aerobic respiration.
A **muscle fibre** is a muscle cell that contracts to produce force.

cards.front: What is myoglobin, and what role does it play in slow twitch fibres?
cards.back: **Myoglobin** is a protein that binds oxygen more tightly than haemoglobin does, storing oxygen inside the fibre as a reserve.
**Glycogen** is a branched polymer of glucose, stored in animal cells, especially in liver and muscle.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say a muscle is made of only one type of fibre?
cards.back: Most muscles contain a **mixture** of slow and fast twitch fibres, and the proportions vary between muscles and between people.

cards.front: Why is it a mistake to think training turns slow twitch fibres into fast twitch fibres?
cards.back: Fibre proportions are largely set by **genes**, so training cannot easily convert one type into the other; it changes how well existing fibres work.
cards.hint: Think about what is fixed before training begins.

cards.front: What changes happen in muscle fibres after endurance training?
cards.back: The fibres gain more **mitochondria** and capillaries, and myoglobin content rises, so aerobic ATP production improves and fatigue sets in later.

cards.front: What changes happen in muscle fibres after sprint and strength training?
cards.back: Each fibre becomes thicker as it gains **contractile protein**, and glycogen stores and anaerobic enzymes increase, so the muscle becomes stronger.

cards.front: Which fibre type suits long-distance running and standing posture, and why?
cards.back: **Slow twitch** fibres, because fatigue resistance matters more than speed when the effort must last for hours.

cards.front: Why does a muscle use slow twitch fibres first during gentle effort?
cards.back: Gentle effort needs only small force for long periods, so **slow twitch** fibres are used first, and **fast twitch** fibres are added when more force is needed.

cards.front: Why does lactate build up quickly in fast twitch fibres?
cards.back: Fast twitch fibres depend on **anaerobic respiration**, which produces lactate quickly, and the resulting fall in pH leads to fatigue.
cards.hint: Compare the ATP source with slow twitch fibres.

cards.front: Why do fast twitch fibres look paler than slow twitch fibres?
cards.back: They have fewer **mitochondria**, less myoglobin and fewer capillaries, so they contain less of the red pigment that gives slow twitch fibres their dark colour.
